newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PM appeals for calm as space probe nears Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PM appeals for calm as space probe nears Australia.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard appealed for calm on Monday as emergency services went on standby to deal with the possible impact of a stricken Russian space probe carrying lethal plutonium.

News that the Mars space probe could fall to Earth in or near Australia came in a telephone call to Howard from U.S. President Bill Clinton, who is due to start an official visit to Australia on Tuesday.
The six-tonne Mars probe, carrying 200 grammes of plutonium in four battery-canisters, blasted off from Kazakhstan on Saturday but failed to make it into orbit around earth.
Clinton aides said the satellite or its debris could come to earth over Australia at around 0100 GMT.

"We want people to know what the situation is, but we don't want people to be melodramatic about it," Howard told reporters after announcing that defence forces across northern and eastern Australia were on alert.

"The public has a right to know that something containing four canisters of plutonium will land in our country -- they must also be reassured that according to the advice we've got, they (the batteries) won't break open," Howard added.
Army and civil defence forces were on emergency standby around Australia, including in the northern state of Queensland and the outback Northern Territory.
The sprawling island-continent is largely uninhabited, except for urban conglomerations on its shores.
Reports conflicted on where the probe could hit Earth, and how much of it would burn up on re-entry through the atmosphere.

Howard told reporters it might land in the Timor Sea between Australia and Indonesia but a U.S. official said it could well come to earth in eastern-central Australia north of Canberra, the country's relatively small political capital.
Howard appeared angry to have heard the news from the United States rather than from Russia itself.
But he said Russian authorities had told Australia the canisters were designed to withstand the heat of re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere and the impact of a crash.
"In which case, there would be no danger of contamination," Howard said.

The possible emergency comes on the eve of a visit by Clinton, his first overseas trip since his November 5 reelection. Clinton will meet Howard on Wednesday and address the Australian parliament before two days of rest in the tropical northern state of Queensland by the Great Barrier Reef.
Howard said Clinton had expressed no reservations about going ahead with his visit, which will be partly a working holiday after the rigours of his re-election.
"He's looking forward to seeing us," Howard said with a laugh. "He's pretty comfortable and relaxed."
U.S. authorities have given Canberra information about the probe and its trajectory and offered help if a clean-up operation is needed.
Australia's space tracking equipment was unable to track the probe, according to a spokesman at the Tidbinbilla satellite tracking station.
Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said teams had begun assembling around the country to implement a pre-organised emergency plan.
The director general of Emergency Management Australia, Alan Hodges, said nuclear emergency teams were standing by as nuclear fallout was considered the greatest danger.
"The radioactive material is not expected to break up, but we have to be sure," Hodges said.
"The Australian defence forces are on standby, but there is no way of telling at this stage where the satellite could land.
"At this stage we are not even sure if any debris will make it to earth ... We have been told it is a small satellite."
In 1979, the United States space laboratory Skylab crashed into Australia's outback, causing no damage.

The unmanned Skylab disintegrated over the desert in Western Australia, near the gold mining town of Kalgoorlie, and two-metre (six-foot) long cylinders weighing half a ton were recovered from the desert.
Australian scientists pointed out that Skylab was tens of metres in diameter, compared with the Russian Mars probe which with its wings totals seven metres (22 feet).
"The Russian space probe itself is only about 2.3 metres (7.6 feet) long," said Tidbinbilla space tracking manager Len Ricardo.
